description: IoT Village at DEF CON 27 covers IoT security vulnerabilities, firmware hacking, and device exploitation. The 14 talks explore attacks on smart home devices, routers, wearables, surveillance cameras, and industrial IoT systems.

talks.title: SOHOpelessly Broken 2 point 0
talks.teaser: Internet of Things (IoT) devices have always been vulnerable to a variety of security issues. In 2013, Independent Security Evaluators (ISE) performed research on IoT devices that showed how rich feature sets could be...
talks.summary:
In this presentation at the DEF CON 27 IoT Village, Rick Ramgattie delivers "SOHOpelessly Broken 2.0," an in-depth review of pervasive vulnerabilities discovered across modern Small Office/Home Office (SOHO) routers and Network Attached Storage (NAS) appliances. He begins at 07:00 by examining host header validation flaws and DNS rebinding attacks that permit external attackers to interact directly with local NAS management interfaces through a victim's browser, bypassing standard NAT firewall protections.

At 14:00, Rick audits web administration consoles across vendors such as Buffalo, TerraMaster, and Netgear, showcasing common software design flaws including unauthenticated command execution and broken access controls in default REST APIs. He recounts the coordinated disclosure process at 21:00, detailing the frustrations of uncommunicative vendors, unresponsive security teams, and instances where vendors silently patched CVEs without publishing security advisories or informing researchers.

At 28:00, Rick analyzes SOAP API vulnerabilities, including instances where firmware blindly trusted client-supplied HTTP headers such as X-Forwarded-For to authenticate administrative requests. He explains his methodology for firmware reverse engineering and binary diffing at 35:00 to identify security patches in new updates. He concludes at 42:00 with a critique of persistent security-through-obscurity practices across IoT consumer hardware and advocates for improved firmware signing and automated vulnerability disclosure standards. talks.title: IoT Security and Manufacturers Q and A Panel
talks.teaser: IoT Security and Manufacturers Q and A Panel
talks.summary:
### Security Challenges Across the IoT Manufacturing Lifecycle
At 00:00, a panel of hardware manufacturers, semiconductor designers, and security researchers convenes at the IoT Village to discuss security challenges across the consumer IoT device lifecycle.

### Insecure Home Routers and Perimeter Devices
At 09:48, the panelists examine vulnerabilities in consumer gateway hardware. They discuss how poorly secured home routers and IoT appliances remain unpatched in residential environments for years, creating large pools of vulnerable devices exploited by botnets.

### Supply Chain Fragmentation and Third-Party Dependencies
At 19:49, the discussion explores supply chain complexities in hardware development. Device manufacturers rely on third-party System-on-Chip (SoC) vendors and open-source software libraries, complicating vulnerability management and long-term patch distribution across product lines.

### Eliminating Attack Surfaces by Design
At 29:52, panelists outline foundational hardware security hygiene. They advocate for disabling physical debug headers (UART/JTAG) before shipping, mandating unique per-device passwords, and integrating hardware root-of-trust chips to support secure boot verification.

### Treating Security as Engineering Quality
Concluding between 40:11 and 48:00, the panel emphasizes that security must be integrated as an essential component of software quality. Panelists urge manufacturers to establish clear vulnerability disclosure programs and implement automated over-the-air update mechanisms to safeguard connected devices over their operational lifespans.

talks.title: Your next roadtrip free - vulnerable EV charging points
talks.teaser: "Electrical Vehicle Charging Points are relatively new on the field and security level of these devices are quite low at the moment. Unfortunately we see lots of EV charging points connected to the internet. This imma...
talks.summary:
In this talk at the DEF CON 27 IoT Village, M. Can Kurnaz presents his vulnerability research into commercial Electric Vehicle (EV) charging stations widely deployed across Europe. He opens at 02:00 by explaining how EV charging infrastructure sits at the critical intersection of IoT and industrial SCADA systems, managing high-voltage electricity and financial billing. At 04:00, he reveals that internet reconnaissance via Shodan uncovered hundreds of public charging stations with their administrative web interfaces directly exposed to the internet.

Can details his web application assessment at 06:00, demonstrating how forced browsing and path traversal allowed unauthenticated visitors to view restricted management pages and device configurations. At 08:00, he illustrates the practical impact of these flaws, showing how an unauthorized remote user could start or stop vehicle charging sessions, alter electricity metering logs, or take charging stations completely offline to strand motorists.

At 10:00, he investigates the internal Java management backend on the charging controller, identifying a remote command injection vulnerability at 12:00 where unescaped backtick commands executed in a shell context. This allowed him to drop directly into an unauthenticated root shell at 14:00, granting full control over the embedded Linux system and network interfaces. He concludes by stressing the urgency of hardening EV charging infrastructure against cyber threats as mass adoption grows. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.teaser: "The IoT industry is often lambasted for lax security, it faces unique challenges. This talk brings expertise from a veteran security engineer who has spent the last few months embedded (pun intended) in an IoT manufa...
talks.summary:
### The State of Insecurity in Consumer Connected Devices
At 00:00, security researcher Lee Brotherston delivers a humorous yet critical overview of recurring security vulnerabilities in consumer Internet of Things (IoT) devices at the IoT Village.

### Insecure Defaults and Physical Exposure
At 05:39, Brotherston critiques fundamental design flaws in consumer smart devices. He highlights the persistence of default administrative passwords, unauthenticated local APIs, and the complete absence of physical tamper resistance on devices deployed in public and residential spaces.

### Hardware Economic Constraints and Margin Pressures
At 11:10, the presentation examines economic pressures shaping IoT development. Tight profit margins on consumer electronics incentivize vendors to minimize hardware costs, leading manufacturers to omit essential flash storage and hardware cryptographic accelerators required for secure communications.

### Bloated Firmware and Outdated Software Components
At 16:26, Brotherston reviews firmware analysis findings across consumer appliances. He demonstrates how manufacturers ship embedded Linux builds containing outdated, vulnerable open-source packages (such as legacy OpenSSL libraries) running as root daemons with full administrative privileges.

### Actionable Design Principles for Hardware Developers
Concluding between 22:05 and 27:29, the speaker outlines practical recommendations for IoT vendors. He calls on developers to minimize software footprints, enforce encrypted communications, implement automated firmware updates, and build products designed to fail safely when network connectivity is lost.

talks.title: Privacy leaks Extracting data from used smart home devices
talks.teaser: "Remember the good old fun sport, where people bought random hard drives from eBay and did forensics on them? Did you know you can do the same thing with used IoT devices too? Most end-users have no idea what kind of ...
talks.summary:
In this comprehensive hardware security talk at the DEF CON 27 IoT Village, Dennis Giese reveals how second-hand smart home devices purchased from online auction sites and thrift stores frequently leak extensive personal and sensitive user data. He begins at 07:00 by exploring why standard "factory reset" functions often fail to sanitize flash storage, leaving gigabytes of residual user data intact across discarded smart vacuum cleaners, smart speakers, Wi-Fi cameras, and IoT hubs.

At 14:00, Dennis breaks down the internal storage architectures of smart devices, explaining the differences between SPI NOR flash, raw NAND flash managed by the Linux Memory Technology Devices (MTD) subsystem, and integrated eMMC chips. He demonstrates physical hardware extraction techniques at 21:00, showing how to attach debug probes to UART serial consoles, solder onto JTAG pins, or read eMMC chips directly using SD card adapters. He also reviews low-cost hardware tools for dumping SPI flash chips at 28:00.

At 35:00, Dennis demonstrates parsing extracted flash file systems (such as SquashFS and UBIFS) to recover original factory credentials, Wi-Fi SSIDs, WPA2 pre-shared keys, and cloud OAuth authentication tokens. In the session's climax at 42:00, he displays sensitive recovered artifacts—including indoor LiDAR floor plans from robot vacuums, camera snapshots, audio recordings, and associated personal identities. He concludes with recommendations for both manufacturers and consumers on how to securely sanitize embedded IoT storage. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Fitbit Firmware Hacking   The Current State of the Heart
talks.teaser: We will show how the Fitbit ecosystem works based on the Fitbit Flex and Fitbit Charge HR as well as the Fitbit Ionic smartwatch. We also show how we modified the firmware of the Fitbit Flex and discuss several vulner...
talks.summary:
Daniel Wegemer presents a detailed hardware and firmware reverse engineering analysis of the Fitbit ecosystem, tracing the architectural evolution from early activity trackers (Fitbit Flex and Charge HR) to the Fitbit Ionic smartwatch. Wegemer breaks down the hardware components of each generation, contrasting the simpler Cortex-M3 ARM microcontroller and Nordic nRF BLE chip of the Flex with the multi-chip architecture of the Ionic, which incorporates a Cypress Bluetooth controller, a Broadcom processor, Wi-Fi, and NFC capabilities.

[07:26] Wegemer details the physical teardown process and hardware modification methodologies, including soldering 39 copper jumper wires onto test points of the Ionic's main PCB to monitor internal buses and tap debug interfaces. He explores firmware extraction, dumping EEPROM contents, and reverse engineering update protocols. For earlier devices like the Flex, he demonstrates remapping GPIO ports over Bluetooth commands to inject custom code and extract firmware images.

[27:38] The presentation turns to the wireless attack surface, investigating the Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) implementation on the Fitbit Ionic. Wegemer highlights legacy diagnostic interfaces carried over from older generations and uncovers security flaws in the Ionic's Bluetooth pairing routines. Specifically, despite running Bluetooth 4.2, the Ionic enforces "Just Works" pairing without user authentication, allowing nearby attackers to sniff communications, manipulate device state, access unencrypted crash dumps, and perform sustained battery drain attacks.

talks.title: Mixing industrial protocols with web application security
talks.teaser: In this talk i'm going to explain in detail a new technique to achieve javascript code persistence in web applications from devices using the Bacnet protocol (building automation) in the underlying device protocol/web...
talks.summary:
In this presentation at the DEF CON 27 IoT Village, Bertin Bervis demonstrates novel attack surfaces that emerge when combining modern web application vulnerabilities with legacy building automation protocols. He begins at 06:00 by challenging the assumption that operational technology networks and building controllers are insulated from web threats due to network air-gapping, showing how internal browsers can be leveraged as proxies to reach internal devices.

Bertin introduces the BACnet protocol architecture at 12:00, examining the BACnet Virtual Link Control (BVLC) and application layer frames used to control HVAC units, smart lighting, and building access points. At 18:00, he demonstrates how an attacker can craft raw binary BACnet packets using standard web technologies, such as Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) and malicious WebSockets executed in a victim's web browser, to bypass firewall and cross-origin boundaries.

At 24:00, Bertin details his testing methodology using real internet-connected building automation controllers. At 30:00, he demonstrates cross-protocol exploitation, where a malicious web page tricks an internal client into delivering BACnet commands to physical building hardware. He highlights command execution vulnerabilities at 36:00 and provides actionable defense-in-depth guidance for network engineers and building operators to isolate industrial protocols from web-facing client networks. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: BITFI You Wouldnt Steal My Cloins
talks.teaser: "Never, ever claim your smart product is unhackable. Don't snort bath salts either. The Bitfi is/was a hardware brain-wallet for crypto currency. John McAfee was probably paid to promote it & wisely identified that it...
talks.summary:
Andrew T delivers a humorous yet technically rigorous teardown of the Bitfi cryptocurrency hardware wallet, a device famously marketed by John McAfee as "completely unhackable" alongside a $250,000 bounty. The talk chronicles how an independent research team analyzed the hardware and dismantled the company's security assertions.

[05:47] An immediate physical inspection reveals that the Bitfi is not custom cryptographic hardware, but rather an inexpensive, repurposed MediaTek Android smartphone stripped of cellular components. Andrew T explains how researchers established communication with the device via exposed serial connections and ADB interfaces, swiftly obtaining root privileges without triggering any hardware tamper mechanisms or defensive wipe routines.

[13:58] The presentation examines Bitfi's "brain-wallet" design, which purported to eliminate cold storage vulnerabilities by recalculating private keys on the fly using a user passphrase and salt. By analyzing RAM during transaction signing and defeating the key-derivation routine, researchers demonstrated full extraction of passphrases, salts, and private keys. The talk concludes with a review of the vendor's controversial responses, public bounty disputes, and the essential security principles—such as secure boot, hardware security modules (HSMs), and transparent threat modeling—absent in the product's design.
